title: The Mystery of Black Holes
text:
Black holes are among the most extreme objects in the universe. They form when massive stars collapse under their own gravity at the end of their lives. The result is a region where gravity is so intense that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses a boundary called the event horizon.

Despite the name, black holes are not empty voids. They contain an enormous amount of mass compressed into an incredibly small space. At the centre lies the singularity, a point where our understanding of physics completely breaks down. Einstein's general relativity predicts its existence but cannot describe what happens there.

Black holes come in different sizes. Stellar black holes form from individual stars and may be only a few times larger than our Sun. Supermassive black holes, found at the centre of most galaxies, can contain billions of solar masses. The black hole at the heart of our galaxy, called Sagittarius A*, has a mass four million times that of our Sun.

For decades, black holes were theoretical. Then in 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope captured the first actual image of a black hole in the galaxy M87. The photograph showed a glowing ring of hot gas surrounding a dark central region.

Time behaves strangely near a black hole, and this is not a metaphor. General relativity predicts that clocks run more slowly in stronger gravity, an effect confirmed daily by satellite navigation systems, which must correct for it to stay accurate. Close to an event horizon the effect becomes extreme. To a distant observer, an object falling in appears to slow, redden and freeze at the boundary, never quite crossing it, while from the falling object's own perspective the crossing happens immediately and unremarkably. Both descriptions are correct, which is one reason black holes are difficult to explain.

Stephen Hawking added a further complication in 1974. Applying quantum theory near the horizon, he calculated that black holes should not be entirely black: they ought to emit a faint radiation and, over unimaginable spans of time, evaporate completely. For a black hole of stellar mass the process would take far longer than the current age of the universe, and the radiation is far too faint to detect. It has never been observed, yet it is widely accepted, because the mathematics is difficult to escape.

A newer method of detection avoids light altogether. When two black holes spiral together and merge, they shake spacetime itself, sending out gravitational waves. In 2015, the LIGO detectors in the United States registered such a signal for the first time, produced by a collision roughly 1.3 billion light years away. The instruments measured a change in length smaller than one ten-thousandth the width of a proton. Each detection lasts less than a second. Since then, hundreds of mergers have been recorded, and astronomy has effectively gained a second sense: events that emit no light at all can now be heard. The signal is usually converted into audible sound so that researchers can listen to it directly.

Scientists study black holes by observing how they affect nearby matter and light. As gas spirals inward, it heats up and emits X-rays that telescopes can detect. Black holes are invisible, but their effects reveal them unmistakably.

title: Living on a Space Station
text:
The International Space Station (ISS) has been continuously inhabited since November 2000, making it humanity's longest-running outpost in space. Orbiting Earth at about 400 kilometres altitude, it travels at 28,000 kilometres per hour and completes 16 orbits of Earth every day.

Life aboard the ISS requires adapting to microgravity, where everything floats unless secured. Astronauts sleep in small sleeping bags attached to walls. They eat specially prepared foods from sealed pouches or cans. Even drinking requires special pouches with straws — ordinary cups would spill in zero gravity.

Water is precious and recycled extensively. The station's systems recover moisture from the air, including water vapour exhaled by the crew, and purify it for drinking. Urine is also recycled into drinking water through advanced filtration processes. Nothing is wasted.

Astronauts must exercise for two hours every day to counteract the muscle and bone loss caused by weightlessness. Despite this, returning astronauts typically need months of rehabilitation on Earth. The longest continuous mission on the ISS lasted 355 days, leaving the astronaut noticeably weakened.

The ISS is also a laboratory. Scientists use the microgravity environment to study biology, physics, and materials science in ways impossible on Earth. Experiments have led to advances in medicine, water purification, and robotics.

The station was not launched; it was assembled. Between 1998 and 2011, more than forty flights carried modules, trusses and solar arrays into orbit, where astronauts joined them together during spacewalks lasting six to eight hours. The finished structure is roughly the size of a football pitch and remains the most expensive object ever built.

Its most unusual feature may be political rather than technical. The ISS is operated jointly by the United States, Russia, Japan, Canada and the European Space Agency, and that cooperation has continued through periods of serious diplomatic hostility between the participating governments. American and Russian crews depend on each other's systems: for years the only route to the station was aboard a Russian Soyuz, and the Russian segment relies on power generated by American solar arrays.

Daily life is stranger than photographs suggest. The station is never quiet, because fans must run constantly — without convection, warm air does not rise, and a sleeping astronaut who did not have moving air would slowly build up a bubble of exhaled carbon dioxide around their own head. Astronauts describe a persistent metallic smell after spacewalks, thought to come from atomic oxygen reacting with the suits. Sunrise happens sixteen times a day, so window blinds and a strict schedule replace daylight as the signal for sleep.

The station will not last indefinitely. Its structure is ageing, small cracks have appeared in the oldest modules, and the current plan is a controlled deorbit around 2030, guiding it into a remote stretch of the southern Pacific Ocean already used as a graveyard for spacecraft. Several private companies have proposed replacement stations, but none has yet flown, and there is a real possibility of a period with no permanently crewed laboratory in orbit for the first time since 2000.

Currently, NASA and its partners are planning a new lunar Gateway station as a stepping stone to Mars, building on lessons learned from over two decades aboard the ISS.

title: Searching for Other Worlds
text:
The discovery of planets beyond our solar system — called exoplanets — has transformed our understanding of the universe. Before 1992, we had no confirmed evidence that other stars hosted planets. Today, astronomers have catalogued over 5,500 exoplanets, with thousands more candidates awaiting confirmation.

Most exoplanets are too far away to photograph directly. Instead, scientists use indirect methods. The transit method detects tiny dips in a star's brightness as a planet passes in front of it, briefly blocking some light. The radial velocity method measures small wobbles in a star caused by a planet's gravitational pull. Both techniques require incredibly precise measurements.

The Kepler Space Telescope, launched in 2009, revolutionised the field by discovering thousands of exoplanets using the transit method. Its successor, the TESS telescope, continues this work today.

Scientists are particularly interested in planets within the habitable zone — the range of distances from a star where liquid water could exist on a planet's surface. Water is considered essential for life as we know it. Several rocky planets in habitable zones have been identified, including some orbiting nearby stars.

The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, can analyse the atmospheres of exoplanets by studying starlight filtered through them. Scientists hope to detect gases like oxygen or methane that might indicate biological processes.

The planets found so far have been stranger than expected. Early surveys were dominated by hot Jupiters — gas giants larger than Jupiter orbiting closer to their star than Mercury does to the Sun, completing a year in a few Earth days. Nobody had predicted them, and their existence forced a rewriting of theories about how planetary systems form, since a giant planet cannot form that close to a star and must therefore have migrated inwards.

The most common type of planet in the galaxy appears to be one the solar system does not contain at all: worlds between the size of Earth and Neptune, often called super-Earths or mini-Neptunes. Whether they are rocky planets with thick atmospheres or small gas planets with deep oceans remains unresolved, and the answer matters, because they are the most abundant places available.

Interpreting an atmosphere is harder than detecting one. Oxygen was long treated as a reliable signature of life, since on Earth it is produced almost entirely by photosynthesis and would otherwise disappear through chemical reactions within a few million years. Astronomers have since identified several processes that could generate oxygen without biology, such as ultraviolet light splitting water vapour on a planet losing its ocean. A single gas is therefore never enough. Researchers now look for combinations that should not coexist — oxygen alongside methane, for instance, since the two destroy each other and their simultaneous presence implies something is continuously replenishing both.

Even a convincing detection would raise a further problem. The nearest confirmed exoplanet in a habitable zone lies about four light years away, which means any signal takes four years to arrive and any visit remains far beyond current propulsion. A probe launched today with existing technology would take tens of thousands of years to arrive.

Whether life exists elsewhere in the universe remains unknown. But with thousands of worlds to examine, the search has never been more promising.

title: The Science of Speedrunning
text:
Most people finish a video game in twenty or thirty hours. Some finish it in eleven minutes. The players who do this are called speedrunners, and what they do turns out to be far more complicated than simply playing quickly.

Speedrunning means completing a game as fast as possible according to rules agreed on by a community. Some categories only require the player to reach the ending by any means available. Others demand that every item is collected first, or that no glitches are used at all. These rules matter enormously, because they decide which shortcuts count as clever and which count as cheating.

The most surprising part of speedrunning is how much of it depends on mistakes — not the player's, but the programmers'. Every large game contains bugs: small errors in the code that nobody noticed before release. Ordinary players almost never meet them. Speedrunners hunt for them deliberately. In one famous platform game, the character can pass straight through a wall if the player jumps at an exact angle on an exact frame, one sixtieth of a second long. Discovering a glitch like that can remove several minutes from a world record overnight.

This is why speedrunning communities look less like sports teams and more like research groups. Runners publish their findings in shared documents, compare recordings frame by frame, and argue about whether a new trick is genuinely faster or merely lucky. When somebody proposes a new route through a game, others test it hundreds of times before it is accepted. A world record is rarely the work of one person. It is usually the last step in years of collective investigation.

Verification is taken seriously. To have a record accepted, a runner must submit an unedited video, and moderators examine it closely for signs of tampering. Cheating scandals do happen. In several well-known cases, runners were found to have spliced together their best attempts or slowed their footage slightly, and their records were deleted. Because the whole system rests on trust, the punishment for breaking it is severe.

Speedrunning has also become a form of charity. Twice a year, an event called Games Done Quick gathers hundreds of runners who play continuously for a week while viewers donate. The event has raised more than fifty million dollars for medical research and disaster relief. Competitors with disabilities take part regularly. One runner completes games using only his feet; another, who is blind, navigates entirely by sound, having memorised the audio cues of every level.

Critics sometimes argue that speedrunning misses the point of games — that racing past a carefully written story wastes the work of the people who made it. Runners tend to disagree. Many say they only speedrun games they already love, and that learning a game deeply enough to break it is its own form of respect. Some developers agree. Several studios now deliberately leave old glitches in place when they release updates, knowing the community depends on them.

What speedrunning ultimately demonstrates is that expertise can grow almost anywhere. The skills involved are patience, precise timing, careful documentation and a willingness to repeat a difficult task thousands of times. Those are the same skills valued in laboratories and workshops. The subject happens to be a video game. The method looks remarkably like science.

title: The Right to Be Heard
text:
In 1989, the United Nations agreed on a treaty that changed how the world talks about childhood. The Convention on the Rights of the Child has been accepted by more countries than any other human rights agreement, and in 2020 Sweden made it part of national law.

The Convention contains fifty-four articles. Some cover what most people would expect: the right to food, shelter, education and medical care. Others are less obvious. Article 31 protects the right to rest and play, a reminder that childhood is not only preparation for adult life. But Article 12 may be the most radical of all. It states that children have the right to express their views on matters that affect them, and that adults must take those views seriously.

Article 12 does not mean that children decide everything. A nine-year-old does not get a vote on whether the family moves to another city. What the article requires is that the child is asked, listened to, and afterwards told how the decision was reached. The difference between being informed and being consulted sounds small. In practice it changes how courts, schools and hospitals work.

Swedish courts now interview children directly in custody cases instead of relying only on what the parents report. Hospitals ask young patients about pain and treatment in ways that were once thought unnecessary. Some municipalities invite pupils onto planning committees when a schoolyard or playground is being redesigned, and the results often differ from what the adults had sketched. In one frequently cited case, the children asked for shelter from rain and corners where small groups could sit, while the adult plan had concentrated almost entirely on equipment for running and climbing.

Progress is uneven. Critics point out that consultation easily becomes decorative: a class is asked for its opinions, the opinions are written down, and nothing changes. Researchers call this tokenism. Genuine participation, they argue, requires that young people know what will happen to what they say and can see the consequences afterwards. Others note that the children most affected by decisions — those in care, those with disabilities, those who have recently arrived in a country — are often the least likely to be asked at all.

There is also disagreement about age. Should a fifteen-year-old have more influence than a seven-year-old? Most legal systems answer yes, but drawing the line is difficult, and the Convention deliberately avoids fixed ages. It refers instead to a child's evolving capacities, a phrase that leaves considerable room for interpretation — and for adults to underestimate what young people actually understand.

Despite these problems, the shift is real. Before 1989, children appeared in international law mainly as objects to be protected. The Convention describes them instead as people whose opinions are worth hearing. Some historians place that change of perspective alongside the abolition of child labour as a turning point in how societies see the young.

The treaty has one striking weakness: enforcement. A committee in Geneva reviews each country's report every five years, but it cannot impose penalties. Its main tool is publicity. States that ignore their obligations are named in reports that journalists and organisations then use to apply pressure. It is a slow instrument. For a document with almost universal support, it depends surprisingly heavily on whether anyone is paying attention.

title: The Wolves That Changed a River
text:
In 1995, fourteen grey wolves were released into Yellowstone National Park in the United States. They were the first wolves in the park for seventy years; the last ones had been shot in the 1920s, when predators were widely regarded as pests. What happened next became one of the most repeated stories in modern nature writing.

Without wolves, the park's elk population had grown very large. The elk grazed heavily along rivers and streams, eating young willow and aspen almost as fast as the trees could grow. When the wolves returned, the elk did not simply decline in number. They also changed their behaviour, avoiding the open valleys where they were easiest to hunt. Trees began to recover in those valleys. Beavers, which need willow, returned and built dams. The dams created ponds for fish and amphibians. Songbirds nested in the new growth. Riverbanks, held together by roots, eroded more slowly, so some streams became narrower and deeper.

Ecologists call this a trophic cascade: a change at the top of a food web that ripples downwards, altering plants, water and landforms. A short film describing the Yellowstone cascade has been watched tens of millions of times, usually under a title claiming that wolves changed the course of rivers.

The science, however, is less tidy than the film. Several researchers who study Yellowstone argue that the story has been simplified almost beyond recognition. Elk numbers were falling for other reasons too, including hunting outside the park, several dry years, and the return of bears and cougars. Willow recovery has been strong in some valleys and barely visible in others. One long-term study found that where groundwater levels had dropped, willows failed to recover even when elk were kept out entirely. The wolves mattered, these scientists say, but they were one factor among many, and the popular version leaves out the complexity that makes the research interesting.

The debate is not only academic, because wolves have returned to Europe as well. After being almost eliminated from Scandinavia, they reappeared in the 1980s and now number a few hundred across Sweden and Norway. Their return has been far more controversial than in Yellowstone, largely because the Scandinavian landscape is not a protected wilderness. It is a working landscape of forestry, farms and hunting grounds.

For a sheep farmer who loses animals, or a hunter whose dog is killed while tracking, the arguments about biodiversity can feel remote. Compensation schemes exist, but they do not cover the effort of rebuilding fences or the anxiety of not knowing what will happen next. Conservation organisations point out that wolves take a very small proportion of livestock compared with disease and traffic, and that the population remains genetically fragile. Both statements can be true at the same time, which is precisely what makes the conflict difficult. Wolves are also protected under European law, which limits how national governments are allowed to respond, and the tension between local frustration and international rules has ended up in court more than once.

What Yellowstone really demonstrates, then, may not be that wolves rebuild rivers. It may be that removing a predator changes a landscape in ways nobody predicted, and that putting one back changes it again — unevenly, slowly, and never quite as neatly as a good story requires.

title: The Understudy
text:
Nadia was given the part nobody wants. Understudy to the lead — which meant learning every line, attending every rehearsal, and almost certainly never going on stage.

"You'll be brilliant," said Ms Okonjo, the drama teacher, in a voice that suggested she knew exactly how disappointing this was. "And if anything happens to Viktor, the whole thing rests on you."

Nothing was going to happen to Viktor. Viktor had played the lead in every production since year seven and had never so much as caught a cold.

What made it harder was the way people assumed Nadia had been given the smaller role because of her hearing. She had worn a hearing aid in her left ear since she was six. It picked up voices well enough in a quiet room, but a rehearsal hall was not a quiet room, and she had learnt long ago to read faces as much as sound. When someone turned away mid-sentence, half the words vanished.

So she developed her own method. She learnt the whole play, not just the lines, but the shape of every scene: who moved where, who breathed before speaking, which gesture came before which cue. While the others waited for their entrances, scrolling on their phones, Nadia sat in the third row with the script open on her knees, watching.

By the fourth week she could predict a fumbled line two seconds before it happened. She began, quietly, to help. She would catch someone in the corridor afterwards. "You come in a bit early on the balcony scene," she'd say. "Wait for him to turn." People started asking her.

Viktor asked her too, which surprised her more than anything. He had the confidence of somebody who has never had to think about how he is perceived, and he used it, one afternoon in November, to say something honest.

"You know the play better than I do."

"I've had more time to watch it."

"That's not what I mean." He rubbed the back of his neck. "I say the words. You understand them."

On the Thursday of performance week, Viktor's grandfather died. Ms Okonjo told the cast in the morning, and the room went very quiet, and then everybody looked at Nadia.

She was not ready. Nobody is ever ready. But she had watched the play ninety times from the third row, and when she stepped into the space where Viktor usually stood, her body already knew where to go.

The difficult part was not the lines. It was the noise: the shuffle of two hundred people, the hum of the lights, the whole soundscape she had never rehearsed in. Twice she lost a cue. Both times she found it by watching — a hand lifting, a step backwards, a mouth opening a fraction early.

Afterwards, her father asked whether she had been frightened, and Nadia thought about it properly before answering.

"Not of forgetting," she said. "I've never been able to rely on hearing my cue anyway. I just watch. Everyone else was suddenly doing what I do all the time."

Viktor came back for the Saturday performance and played the lead, and he was very good. But at the curtain call he stepped back and gestured towards the third row, where Nadia had returned to sit with the script open on her knees, and the applause went on considerably longer than anyone expected.

title: The Complaint on the Third Floor
text:
The letter was taped to the door of the rehearsal room, printed in a font so large it could be read from the stairs.

THE NOISE FROM THIS ROOM ON TUESDAYS AND THURSDAYS IS UNREASONABLE. THIS IS THE FOURTH TIME I HAVE WRITTEN.

No signature, but everybody knew. Mr Bergqvist, third floor, the flat directly above the community centre's music room. He had complained about the guitar amplifier in September, the singing in October, and now, apparently, about existence in general.

"He's eighty-something," said Amira, unpacking her bass. "My mum says he never leaves the building."

"He leaves to complain," said Theo.

They had been rehearsing for eleven weeks for a competition none of them expected to win, and they were not, Amira privately admitted, very good. The drums rushed. The bass and guitar disagreed about where beat one was. Their singer, Milla, had a strong voice and no idea what to do with it.

On the third Thursday after the letter, someone knocked. Not the caretaker's knock — three quick raps, then silence.

Mr Bergqvist was shorter than Amira had imagined, and he was holding a piece of paper. Everyone braced.

"Your drummer," he said, "is playing on top of the beat. Not behind it. On top of it. That is why the whole thing sounds like an argument."

Nobody spoke.

"It's not the volume," he added, more quietly. "I don't mind the volume. It's that you've been making the same mistake for eleven weeks and I have had to listen to all of them."

Theo, who had been playing drums for four years and had never received a note from anybody, said: "How would you fix it?"

So Mr Bergqvist came in and sat on the plastic chair by the door, and for twenty minutes he did not touch an instrument. He clapped. He counted. He asked Theo to play only the hi-hat, then only the kick drum, then to leave a gap where he had been putting an extra note. The song, unmistakably, stopped arguing with itself.

He had been a session drummer, it turned out, for twenty-six years. Studios in Stockholm and Copenhagen, mostly, backing singers whose names Milla had to look up afterwards and then repeated in disbelief. His hands had stopped cooperating in his sixties — arthritis, he said, in the same tone he might have used for the weather — and he had not played since.

He came the following Tuesday without being invited. Then every Tuesday. He never brought sticks. He sat on the plastic chair with a coffee, counted quietly along, and occasionally offered one sentence that reorganised the entire afternoon.

They came fourth in the competition, which was three places better than anyone had predicted and, according to Milla, entirely because of the eight bars of silence Mr Bergqvist had made them put before the last chorus. "Nobody your age trusts a gap," he had told them. "You think silence is where the music stops. It's where it gets ready."

Amira taped something to the rehearsal room door after that, in the same enormous font he had used.

THE NOISE FROM THIS ROOM ON TUESDAYS AND THURSDAYS IS SIGNIFICANTLY IMPROVED. PLEASE CONTINUE COMPLAINING.

He left it up for a year.

title: Muhammad Ali's Early Life
text:
Muhammad Ali was born as Cassius Marcellus Clay Jr. in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1942. He grew up during a period when racial segregation affected many parts of American society. As a child, he was energetic, confident, and highly competitive. According to a well-known story, his interest in boxing began after his bicycle was stolen when he was twelve years old. Angry about the theft, he told a police officer that he wanted to fight the person responsible. The officer, who also trained young boxers, suggested that he first learn how to box. Clay quickly became dedicated to the sport and spent many hours practicing. His natural speed, quick reflexes, and determination helped him improve rapidly. During his teenage years, he won several amateur competitions and developed a boxing style that was different from many fighters of the time. Instead of relying mainly on power, he used movement, timing, and footwork. His success eventually earned him a place on the United States Olympic boxing team. At the 1960 Olympic Games in Rome, he won a gold medal in the light heavyweight division. The victory brought him national attention and opened the door to a professional career. Soon after turning professional, he continued winning matches and attracting media interest. Unlike many athletes, Clay openly predicted his victories and spoke confidently about his abilities. Some people found his behavior entertaining, while others considered it arrogant. However, his confidence helped create public interest in his fights. As his reputation grew, he faced stronger opponents and continued to prove himself in the ring. His combination of athletic skill, intelligence, and charisma made him one of the most talked-about young athletes in the United States. These early experiences shaped the person he would become. The policeman who suggested boxing was called Joe Martin, and he ran a gym in the basement of Columbia Auditorium as well as a television programme called Tomorrow's Champions. Clay appeared on it repeatedly. By the time he was eighteen he had fought more than a hundred amateur bouts and won two national Golden Gloves titles.

The 1960 Games nearly did not happen for him. Clay was afraid of flying and initially refused to board the aircraft to Rome. He was persuaded only after buying a parachute at an army surplus store and wearing it for the entire flight.

Rome suited him. He talked constantly, collected addresses from athletes of other countries, and was photographed so often that a journalist called him the mayor of the Olympic Village. He won the light heavyweight final against a Polish opponent and afterwards wore the medal everywhere, including to bed.

Louisville received him warmly and then reminded him where he was. Accounts differ about the details, but Clay described being refused service in a restaurant while still wearing the gold medal, and the moment recurs in almost everything he later said about that period. Whether or not it happened exactly as he told it, the point he drew from it did not change: a medal earned for a country did not alter how that country treated him at a counter in his own city.

The challenges he faced as a young African American, his dedication to training, and his willingness to stand out from others all contributed to his future success. Before he became a world champion and a global icon, he was a determined teenager who transformed a difficult moment into the beginning of an extraordinary career.

title: Becoming Muhammad Ali
text:
After establishing himself as a successful professional boxer, Cassius Clay experienced important personal changes that influenced the rest of his life. During the early 1960s, he became interested in the Nation of Islam, a religious and political movement that focused on Black identity, self-respect, and social change. At a time when racial discrimination remained a major issue in the United States, many African Americans were searching for ways to challenge inequality and gain greater recognition. Clay listened carefully to the movement's ideas and eventually decided to join. Following his victory over Sonny Liston in 1964, he announced that he would no longer use the name Cassius Clay. Instead, he adopted the name Muhammad Ali. The decision attracted widespread attention and generated strong reactions. Supporters viewed the change as an expression of religious freedom and personal identity. Critics argued that he was rejecting traditions associated with his earlier life. Ali remained firm in his decision despite the controversy. He believed that choosing his own name allowed him to define himself rather than accept labels imposed by others. His willingness to defend his beliefs became one of the most recognizable aspects of his public image. Beyond boxing, he increasingly spoke about race, religion, and equality. This was unusual for many athletes at the time because public figures often avoided political topics. Ali's comments sometimes made him controversial, but they also earned him respect from people who admired his honesty. His growing influence demonstrated that athletes could shape public discussions as well as sporting events. The name Muhammad Ali eventually became known around the world. It represented more than a personal choice; it symbolized independence and self-determination. Historians often note that the decision reflected broader social changes occurring during the civil rights era. By openly embracing a new identity, Ali showed that success in sports did not require abandoning personal convictions. Instead, he used his fame to communicate ideas that mattered to him. The change happened in two stages. Immediately after the Liston fight he announced that he would be known as Cassius X, discarding what he called a slave name while awaiting one from the Nation of Islam. Elijah Muhammad gave him the name Muhammad Ali some weeks later, and explained that it meant beloved of God.

Much of the boxing world simply refused to use it. Newspapers continued printing Cassius Clay for years, some for a decade. Promoters announced him under the old name. The refusal was rarely explained, which made its meaning clearer: to accept the name was to accept that a Black athlete could define himself.

The dispute became physical in 1967. Ernie Terrell, before their fight, repeatedly called him Clay in interviews. Ali won the fight decisively and prolonged it, shouting the same question between combinations: What is my name? Sportswriters found the display cruel, and several who had defended him previously turned against him afterwards.

Ali did not apologise for it, then or later. He argued that a man who insists on calling you by a name you have rejected is not making a small mistake but a large statement, and that he had answered in the only language available inside a boxing ring.

Whether people agreed with him or not, many recognized the courage required to take such a public stand. The transformation from Cassius Clay to Muhammad Ali marked a turning point in his life and helped establish his legacy as both an athlete and a social figure.

When did he announce his new name?
How did supporters view the name change?
What made Ali unusual among athletes of the time?
options: His willingness to discuss social issues

title: The Vietnam War Controversy
text:
One of the most significant moments in Muhammad Ali's life occurred during the Vietnam War. In 1967, the United States government expected eligible men to serve in the military through the draft system. Ali refused induction into the armed forces. He explained that his religious beliefs and personal principles prevented him from participating in the conflict. His position immediately became the subject of national debate. Some Americans considered his refusal unpatriotic and believed that public figures should support military service during wartime. Others argued that he had the right to follow his conscience and practice his religion freely. The consequences for Ali were severe. He was stripped of his heavyweight boxing title and lost his boxing license in many states. As a result, he was unable to compete professionally during some of the most productive years of his athletic career. In addition, he faced legal challenges that threatened his freedom and financial stability. Despite these difficulties, Ali continued to defend his position. He spoke publicly about his beliefs and accepted the risks associated with his decision. Over time, opinions about the issue began to change. As public attitudes toward the Vietnam War became more critical, some people started viewing Ali's actions differently. In 1971, the United States Supreme Court overturned his conviction, allowing him to return fully to professional boxing. Historians often describe this episode as an important example of the relationship between sports, politics, and individual rights. Ali's choice demonstrated that athletes can influence discussions far beyond their own professions. His actions continue to generate debate because they raise questions about citizenship, responsibility, and freedom of conscience. Supporters emphasize the courage required to sacrifice a successful career in defense of personal principles. Critics maintain that national obligations should take priority during times of conflict. Regardless of perspective, the event remains a defining chapter in Ali's life. The refusal itself took only a moment. At the induction ceremony in Houston in April 1967, Ali stood still when his name was called. He was asked a second time and did not move. That was the whole act.

The consequences arrived within an hour. The New York State Athletic Commission suspended his licence the same day, before any trial had taken place, and other states followed. In June he was convicted of draft evasion, sentenced to five years in prison and fined ten thousand dollars. He remained free on appeal, but he could not leave the country and could not fight anywhere in the United States.

He was twenty-five, and the exile lasted three and a half years — most of what would have been his physical peak. He supported himself by speaking at universities, where he was often the first person the audience had heard argue the case against the war directly.

The Supreme Court decision in 1971 was narrower than it is usually remembered. The justices did not rule on conscientious objection in general. They found that the appeal board had failed to state which of three legal grounds it had used to reject his claim, and that this procedural failure made the conviction unsound. The vote was unanimous. By then he had already lost the years the ruling could not return.

It showed that he was willing to accept significant personal costs rather than compromise his beliefs. The controversy also contributed to his lasting reputation as a figure whose impact extended beyond the boxing ring and into broader discussions about justice and individual freedom.

title: The Rumble in the Jungle
text:
In 1974, Muhammad Ali participated in one of the most famous boxing matches in history. The event, later known as the Rumble in the Jungle, took place in Kinshasa, Zaire, which is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Ali's opponent was George Foreman, the reigning heavyweight champion. Many experts predicted that Foreman would win. He was younger, stronger, and had recently defeated several leading fighters. Ali entered the match as the underdog. Rather than relying on a traditional strategy, he adopted an approach that surprised both spectators and commentators. During much of the fight, he leaned against the ropes and allowed Foreman to throw large numbers of punches. This tactic became known as the "rope-a-dope." Although it appeared risky, Ali believed it would tire his opponent. As the rounds progressed, Foreman began losing energy. Ali carefully observed the situation and waited for the right moment to attack. In the eighth round, he launched a series of fast and accurate punches that knocked Foreman to the canvas. The victory shocked many observers and restored Ali's status as heavyweight champion. Beyond its sporting significance, the fight attracted international attention. It highlighted the growing global popularity of boxing and brought focus to an African nation that many people outside the continent knew little about. The event also demonstrated Ali's intelligence as a competitor. Instead of depending solely on physical strength, he used strategy, patience, and psychological insight. Sports historians frequently cite the match as evidence of his exceptional understanding of boxing. The Rumble in the Jungle became an important part of Ali's legacy because it showed his ability to overcome difficult odds. It remains one of the most analyzed contests in sports history. The fight took place in Zaire because its ruler, Mobutu Sese Seko, paid for it. He put up ten million dollars, an enormous sum in 1974, to have the event staged in Kinshasa and broadcast worldwide, on the reasoning that the publicity would present his government favourably. Journalists at the time noted the arrangement; several also noted what happened to political opponents in the same city.

The fight was delayed five weeks after Foreman was cut above the eye in training, which left both boxers stranded in Kinshasa. Ali used the time. He appeared constantly in public, learned a phrase in Lingala — Ali, boma ye, meaning Ali, kill him — and taught it to crowds until they chanted it wherever he went. Foreman, who kept largely to his quarters and travelled with a German shepherd, later observed that the dog was the breed the Belgian colonial police had used, and that he had understood too late how the crowd would read it.

It began at four in the morning, so that American television could broadcast it in the evening.

Foreman's own account of the fight has grown more generous over the decades. He has said that he punched himself out against a man who had decided in advance to let him, that he did not understand what was happening until the seventh round, and that he had never before met an opponent who talked to him while being hit. He has also said, more than once, that losing it was the best thing that happened to him.

Even decades later, athletes and coaches continue to study the fight for lessons about preparation, adaptability, and decision-making under pressure. The victory reinforced Ali's reputation as a champion capable of succeeding in situations where many expected him to fail.

What is the main idea of the passage?

title: Muhammad Ali's Legacy
text:
Muhammad Ali is remembered not only as one of the greatest boxers of all time but also as a global cultural figure. His achievements inside the ring were extraordinary. He won world heavyweight championships, defeated many leading opponents, and became famous for his speed, skill, and confidence. However, his influence extended far beyond sports. Throughout his life, Ali used his public platform to discuss issues such as equality, religion, and human dignity. As a result, he became an important figure in conversations about social change. After retiring from boxing, Ali remained active in public life. He traveled internationally, participated in humanitarian projects, and supported charitable causes. In later years, he lived with Parkinson's disease, a neurological condition that affected his movement and speech. Despite these challenges, he continued appearing at public events and inspiring people around the world. Many admired the determination he showed while dealing with illness. One of the most memorable moments of his later life occurred during the opening ceremony of the 1996 Olympic Games in Atlanta, where he lit the Olympic cauldron. The image became a powerful symbol of resilience and perseverance. Historians, athletes, and journalists often debate which aspect of Ali's legacy is most important. Some emphasize his accomplishments as a boxer, while others focus on his willingness to defend his beliefs during periods of controversy. Many argue that his greatest contribution was demonstrating that athletes can influence society in meaningful ways. His life story continues to be studied because it connects sports with larger themes such as courage, identity, justice, and leadership. Schools, documentaries, and museums frequently examine his impact on both American and global history. Even people with little interest in boxing often recognize his name and understand his significance. Muhammad Ali's legacy endures because he achieved excellence in competition while also engaging with important social issues. His illness complicated his legacy in a way he seemed to accept. Parkinson's disease was diagnosed in 1984, three years after his final fight, and although the condition can arise without any head injury, neurologists have consistently linked repeated blows to a raised risk. Ali was asked about it often. He declined to blame boxing, saying he would have made the same choices, but his visible decline became one of the strongest arguments the sport's critics possessed, and he did not object when others used it that way.

The 1996 Olympic ceremony in Atlanta was kept secret until the moment it happened. Organisers had considered several candidates to light the cauldron. When Ali stepped out, shaking badly, holding the torch with obvious difficulty, the stadium reaction was so prolonged that the broadcast schedule was disrupted. Many viewers had not seen him in years.

Public opinion had by then reversed almost completely. The man who was stripped of his title in 1967, and whom a majority of Americans told pollsters they disapproved of, received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2005. Historians frequently point out that this reversal required no change from Ali himself. He held the same positions throughout. What changed was the country's assessment of the war he had refused to fight, and of the question he had been asking about who owed what to whom.

His example encourages people to pursue their goals, think independently, and remain committed to their values. For these reasons, he remains one of the most influential sporting figures of the twentieth century and an enduring symbol of determination and principle.

title: What the Mirror Didn't Say
text:
The first thing people noticed about Vincent was that he was funny. He had discovered early that a well-timed joke worked like a shield: if people were laughing, they weren't looking too closely. By ninth grade, he had perfected the act. Class clown, always on, always fine.

The truth was less entertaining. The truth was lying awake at two in the morning rehearsing conversations that would never happen. The truth was the knot in his stomach every Sunday evening, and the exhausting daily performance of being okay.

It was Ms. Lindgren, the art teacher, who noticed. Not because he stopped joking — he never stopped joking — but because of a self-portrait he'd painted in October. The assignment was to paint yourself as others see you. Most students produced flattering selfies in acrylic. Vincent painted a grinning mask, and behind it, barely visible in greys, a second face that wasn't grinning at all.

She kept him after class. He prepared a joke about modern art being open to interpretation. She looked at the painting, then at him, and said: "You know the assignment was how others see you. This looks more like how others don't."

The joke evaporated. For a horrible, liberating moment, Vincent had nothing funny to say.

They talked for an hour. Then she walked with him to the school counsellor's office and waited until he went in. The counsellor's name was Farid, and the first thing he said was that Vincent did not have to talk if he did not want to, which was so unexpected that Vincent talked for forty minutes.

It went badly at first. Vincent was good at conversation in the way that people who use it as cover are good at it, and he spent two sessions being charming, funny and entirely uninformative. Farid did not interrupt. In the third session he said that Vincent was doing something he saw often, and asked whether he wanted to know what it was.

"Go on."

"You are managing me. You are checking whether I am all right, in a room where you are the one who is supposed to be all right."

Vincent said nothing for a long time, which was itself unusual.

The months after that were unremarkable in a way nobody warns you about. There was no breakthrough. There were appointments, some useful and some not, a period of feeling worse before feeling better, and a conversation with his parents that he had rehearsed for three weeks and that lasted four minutes, because they had, it turned out, been waiting for him to start it.

He kept joking. That surprised him most. He had assumed the humour was the illness, and that recovering meant giving it up, but it turned out the jokes were his and the hiding was the problem, and the two could be separated.

Ms Lindgren gave him the painting back at the end of the year. She had kept it in the store cupboard, in case he wanted it. He did. It hung in his room for a decade, mask outwards, because the second face was only visible if you already knew to look for it.

It wasn't a cure — those took longer, he would learn. But years later, Vincent would still think of that painting as the most honest thing he made in school: the day the mask came off, because one person had bothered to look behind it.

title: The Whistle
text:
Amir had refereed forty-one matches in the youth league, and he could feel a bad one coming the way sailors feel weather. This one announced itself early: parents pressing against the touchline, a coach who disputed the first throw-in, and a number nine who played with his elbows.

In the second half, with the score tied, the number nine went down in the penalty area. Theatrically. Hopefully. The home crowd roared for a penalty.

Amir had seen it clearly: no contact. He waved play on.

What followed was ugly. The coach screamed. A parent called him a cheat, then something worse — something about where he was 'really from'. The match finished 2–2, and Amir walked to the changing room with his jaw clenched, forty kronor richer and several illusions poorer. He was sixteen years old.

He almost quit that evening. The email was half-written when his phone buzzed. Unknown number. "Hi. My son played number six today, the tall one. He told me what that parent shouted at you. He also said you were the best ref they've had all season — you saw the dive everyone else missed. People who scream are loud, but they're not the majority. Hope you stay."

Amir read it three times. Then he deleted the email draft and opened next weekend's fixture list instead.

The league lost forty per cent of its referees under twenty within three years, and nobody found this mysterious. Exit interviews, when anyone bothered to conduct them, said the same thing repeatedly: not the difficulty of the decisions, not the running, not the early mornings. Abuse from adults.

Amir stayed, and afterwards was never entirely sure why. He had the message from the parent, which he kept. He also had a stubbornness that he did not experience as courage at the time and would not describe that way later.

He got better. That part is rarely mentioned in discussions about abuse, and it matters, because the second season was easier than the first for reasons that had nothing to do with thicker skin. He learned to explain a decision in four words while walking away, which prevented most arguments from starting. He learned that where he stood determined what he saw, and that most disputed calls come from being in the wrong position ninety seconds earlier. He learned to talk to the captain rather than the crowd.

There was one more incident, in his fourth year. A coach followed him toward the changing room after a match, still shouting. Amir did what the guidance said: he stopped, said nothing, and wrote it down afterwards in detail.

The report went nowhere for five months. Then the district, under pressure from a group of clubs, suspended the coach for six matches, and the decision was published with his name in it. Amir had not expected that. Several referees he had never met sent him messages.

That was the year he stopped thinking of himself as someone who happened to referee.

He still lost matches to the shouting. Two seasons later he abandoned a game after fifteen minutes because a touchline would not quieten, walked to the centre circle, picked up the ball and left. Half the parents complained. The other half apologised.

He refereed for nine more years, and eventually, the league's young referees got a mentor programme. Amir ran it. The first thing he taught new referees wasn't the rulebook. It was this: "The screamers are loud. They are not the majority. Now, let's talk about offside."

title: Driving Lessons
text:
My mother taught me to drive the summer she got sick, which tells you everything about her. Other people, receiving that kind of news, might have postponed things. She accelerated them.

"Mirror, signal, manoeuvre," she said from the passenger seat of our old Volvo, on a gravel road where the worst I could hit was a hay bale. "And relax your shoulders. You drive like you're being chased."

We went out every Tuesday and Thursday that summer. I learned hill starts while she quizzed me about my future. I learned parallel parking while she told stories I'd never heard — about hitchhiking through Portugal at nineteen, about the motorcycle she'd owned before I was born and sold, she claimed, 'under protest and under pressure.'

I understood what she was doing. She was downloading herself into me, lesson by lesson, while pretending it was about clutch control. I let her pretend. Some conversations can only happen sideways, both people facing the windscreen, the engine giving you something to do with your hands.

She was there when I passed my test the following spring — thinner by then, in a wheelchair she called 'temporary' long past the point anyone believed it. I drove her home from the test centre myself. She criticised my lane changes the entire way, and I have never loved anyone more.

There is a version of that summer I could tell in which we discussed it. We did not. Not once, in eleven weeks, did either of us say the word.

Instead she told me about Portugal. She was nineteen, she had eleven pounds, and she hitchhiked from Faro to Porto with a woman she had met on a bus who turned out to be running away from a marriage. She told me about the Honda she had bought with her first proper wage, and was vague about why she sold it, in a way that suggested the story existed and was not being told.

She told me about her own mother teaching her to drive, how badly it had gone, and how she had promised herself she would do it differently. I understood that she was giving me a version of an inheritance. I did not understand it fast enough to say anything useful.

What I said instead, mostly, was that she was making me nervous, and could she please stop commenting on my mirror checks.

She got worse in February. By March she was using the wheelchair. She still came out on Tuesdays, from the passenger seat, correcting my lane discipline with a voice that had less air behind it every week, and I kept driving the same three roads because I could not think of a way to say that I did not want the lessons to end. She never suggested a different route either.

She was there when I passed my test in April. She criticised my parking on the way home, and I have never loved anyone more.

The last lesson was in March. We drove to the water and sat with the engine off while she got her breath back, and she said that I was a better driver than she had been at my age. It is the only compliment from that year I still hear in her voice.

She didn't see the autumn. But every time I start a car, I hear it — mirror, signal, manoeuvre, relax your shoulders. People leave us in pieces, I've learned. And some of the pieces are instructions.

title: The Animal That Built Our World
text:
Few animals have shaped human history as profoundly as the horse. For most of the past five thousand years, the horse was our fastest form of transport, our strongest farm worker, and our most decisive military technology — all in one animal.

Horses were first domesticated on the grasslands of Central Asia, probably around 3500 BCE. The consequences were enormous. Distances that had taken weeks to cross on foot could suddenly be covered in days. Ideas, languages, goods, and unfortunately also diseases began moving across continents at a completely new speed. Some historians argue that the horse was the most important 'communication technology' before the printing press.

In warfare, cavalry dominated battlefields for millennia, from ancient chariots to the mounted armies of the Mongol Empire, which in the 1200s built the largest connected land empire in history — largely on horseback. In agriculture, horses pulled the ploughs that fed growing cities. In everyday life, they pulled carriages, delivered post, and hauled goods through city streets. As late as 1900, cities like London and New York were utterly dependent on tens of thousands of working horses.

Then, within a few decades, the combustion engine changed everything. Cars, tractors, and trucks took over the horse's work. The transformation was so complete that we still measure engine power in 'horsepower' — a ghost of the world the horse built.

Yet the horse did not disappear. Instead, its role changed from worker to companion. Today, millions of horses live as partners in sport, therapy, and recreation. In Sweden, horse riding is one of the largest youth sports, and riding schools are often described as leadership schools: caring for a large, powerful animal teaches responsibility, calm, and clear communication in a way few other activities can.

Two numbers illustrate how recently this changed. In 1900, London required roughly three hundred thousand working horses to function, and the manure they produced was considered one of the city's most urgent public health problems, with newspapers predicting that streets would eventually become impassable. Within twenty-five years the problem had disappeared entirely, replaced by a different set of exhaust products that nobody yet worried about.

The First World War was the last conflict in which horses were central and the first in which that was clearly a mistake. Britain alone sent more than a million horses to the front. Only a small fraction returned. Cavalry charges against machine guns produced casualties that ended the tactic permanently, while the animals that survived were used for hauling artillery through mud that defeated early motor vehicles.

The modern relationship is different in kind, not just in scale. Equine-assisted therapy is now used in the treatment of anxiety, trauma and autism, and the reasoning is specific rather than sentimental: a horse is large enough that it cannot be ignored, responds immediately to a handler's tension, and offers no social pretence. A person who is anxious gets an anxious horse, and the feedback arrives without judgement or delay.

Riding schools describe a similar effect without the clinical vocabulary. An animal weighing half a tonne does not cooperate because it is asked politely. It cooperates when instructions are clear and consistent, which is a demanding standard for a twelve-year-old, and an unusually honest one. Instructors say the animal teaches the lesson faster than any adult can explain it.

The horse no longer pulls our world forward. But for five thousand years, it did exactly that.

title: The Fans Who Would Not Wait
text:
Harry Potter arrived at the same time as the household internet, and the two shaped each other. The series was the first enormous children's phenomenon to have a gap of years between instalments and a generation of readers with message boards. What filled that gap became a model for almost every fandom since.

The waiting was the engine. Between books, readers had nothing new to read and a great deal to argue about, so they produced their own material. Fan fiction ran into millions of stories on sites built specifically to hold them. Some writers who began there now publish professionally, and several have said that an audience of strangers giving detailed feedback taught them more than any course. There were also fan-made films, illustrated encyclopaedias, and a small genre of guitar music written from the point of view of the characters.

Theory was the other half. Readers compiled every detail the author had let slip and argued from it, sometimes for years. Long essays predicted the loyalties of particular characters from single sentences in earlier books. When the final volume appeared, some of these predictions turned out to be right, which had the odd effect of making the readers feel they had solved something rather than been told it.

The author encouraged this. Rowling answered questions online, confirmed and denied theories, and gave interviews that added facts not present in the novels. That raised a question the fandom argued about for years: does something count if it is not in the book? Some readers accepted every statement. Others held that the text is the text, and that an author explaining her own work afterwards is just another reader with an opinion.

Publishers watched all of this closely, because it broke a rule they had believed in. Rights holders had traditionally treated fan work as theft and issued legal threats. Here, the fan activity was clearly increasing sales, and the tolerant approach that emerged became the industry norm.

Not all of it was harmless. Fan communities produced their own hierarchies, and the largest sites had moderators with real power over who was read and who was ignored. Arguments about theories became personal, and some of them lasted years. A subgroup of readers treated the books as a set of facts to be catalogued rather than a story to be interpreted, which is a recognisable way of reading, and not always a generous one. There were also disputes over what belonged on public sites at all, given that many of the writers and most of the readers were children.

The commercial edge blurred too. Fan sites accepted advertising, some ran conventions with paid tickets, and a few of the largest were eventually bought by media companies. What had begun as unpaid enthusiasm turned, in places, into a small industry, and the people who had built the archives did not always benefit from the sale. Later fandoms inherited both the tools and the arguments about who owns them.

The wider effect was on how audiences behave. Before this, being a fan mostly meant consuming something and perhaps joining a club. Afterwards it meant producing: writing, drawing, recording, arguing in public and building archives that outlived the wait. Series released today are designed with that in mind, with gaps left deliberately for the audience to fill. Whether that makes for better stories is arguable. That it changed the relationship between a book and its readers is not.

title: How Manga Left Japan
text:
For most of its history, manga was made for Japanese readers and nobody else. Today it is one of Japan's largest cultural exports, sold in dozens of languages, and the route it took was not planned by anyone.

The first serious English editions appeared in the late 1980s, and they were altered heavily. Because English is read from left to right, publishers mirrored every page so that the story ran the familiar way. This solved one problem and created several others. Mirrored characters became left-handed. Writing in the background appeared backwards. Any drawing that depended on which side of the frame a character stood on now said something slightly different. Artists complained, and one of them, Akira Toriyama, is reported to have objected to the flipping of his work.

The change came in 2002, when the publisher Tokyopop began printing unflipped volumes at a lower price, marketed with the claim that this was the authentic form. The gamble was that readers would accept an unfamiliar reading direction if the alternative was waiting or paying more. They did. Within a few years right-to-left printing had become the standard, and a small note explaining it appears in the back of almost every English volume.

Translation raised harder questions. Japanese has levels of politeness with no English equivalent, and honorifics attached to names carry information about age and closeness that a translation must either keep, explain or discard. Sound words are drawn into the artwork, so replacing them means altering the picture. Food, school customs and holidays can be adapted for a foreign reader or left as they are with a note at the back, and publishers still disagree about which is better.

Meanwhile readers had stopped waiting. Groups of fans began scanning Japanese volumes, translating them and posting the results online, often within a day of publication. This practice, known as scanlation, was clearly illegal, and it was also the reason many series found an audience abroad at all. Publishers spent years fighting it before concluding that the real answer was speed, and several magazines now release official English chapters on the same day as the Japanese edition.

Animation did much of the early work. A television series could be dubbed, sold cheaply to foreign broadcasters and shown to children who had never heard of manga, and by the 1990s a generation in Europe and North America had grown up on Japanese cartoons without knowing where the stories came from. When those viewers discovered that the episodes were adapted from books, a market existed before anyone had marketed anything.

Libraries were an unexpected ally. Manga is cheap, borrowed constantly and read by teenagers who borrow little else, and by the 2010s many school and public libraries in Europe were building collections deliberately. Some now stock more manga than any other kind of fiction. Teachers who had once treated comics as a distraction began using them with students who found long prose difficult, which changed the medium's reputation faster than any publisher could have.

The market has followed. Manga now accounts for a large share of graphic novel sales in North America and Europe, and Japanese publishers plan for foreign readers from the beginning rather than treating them as an afterthought. A medium that was designed for cheap magazines on Japanese commuter trains ended up shaping what young people read on the other side of the world, largely because its own readers refused to wait for permission.

title: The Bystander Effect, and What Was Wrong With It
text:
In 1964 a woman named Kitty Genovese was murdered outside her building in New York. Two weeks later a newspaper reported that thirty-eight neighbours had watched from their windows and that not one of them had called the police. The story spread quickly, and psychologists began asking what it was about a crowd that made people do nothing.

The experiments that followed became some of the most famous in the subject. In one, students sat alone in rooms and spoke to each other through an intercom. One of the voices, which was in fact a recording, began to describe a seizure. Students who believed they were the only listener went for help almost every time. Students who believed four other people could also hear went for help far less often, and those who did took much longer.

The explanation offered was diffusion of responsibility. In a group, the duty to act is divided, and each person can assume someone else is already dealing with it. A second factor is that people watch each other for clues. If nobody else looks alarmed, the situation is read as less serious than it is, even when everybody privately feels uneasy.

The finding entered textbooks, driving lessons and safety courses, usually in the same blunt form: the more witnesses there are, the less likely you are to be helped. It sounded like a warning about modern indifference, and it was repeated for decades.

Then the original story fell apart. Journalists and historians who examined the court records found that the figure of thirty-eight witnesses was wrong. Most of the neighbours heard something without seeing anything, few could tell what was happening in the dark, at least one did call the police, and a woman went out into the street and held Genovese as she died. The article that started the whole field was, in large part, inaccurate.

The experiments themselves were more solid, but they too have been reconsidered. A large review published in 2019 examined more than two hundred recordings of real conflicts caught on public cameras in three countries. Someone intervened in about nine cases out of ten. More strikingly, the chance of receiving help went up, not down, as the number of people present increased. Bigger crowds contained more people willing to step in.

Why did the original version last so long? Partly because it was useful. A single dramatic story is easier to teach than a set of qualified findings, and the number thirty-eight gave it the appearance of precision. Partly, too, because it flattered a certain view of city life. Readers in the 1960s were already worried that urban living made people cold, and the article confirmed what they suspected.

The practical advice has changed as a result. Safety courses once told people to shout at one specific person in a crowd, on the theory that a general appeal would be ignored by everyone. That instruction still works, and it costs nothing, but it is now taught alongside a different message: most people do help, and the person most likely to intervene is someone who has thought about it beforehand.

The bystander effect has not disappeared. It appears reliably in ambiguous situations, where nobody is certain that anything is wrong. But the general claim that crowds make people passive is not supported by what actually happens on the street, and the safety advice built on it has begun to change with the evidence.

title: The Impact of Globalization on Culture
text:
Globalization has transformed societies around the world by increasing the movement of goods, ideas, technology, and people across national borders. Supporters of globalization argue that international cooperation and trade have improved economic development, expanded cultural exchange, and increased access to information. Critics, however, warn that globalization may weaken local traditions and increase economic inequality.

One major effect of globalization can be seen in popular culture. Music, films, fashion, and social media trends now spread rapidly between countries. Young people in different parts of the world often consume similar entertainment and communicate through the same digital platforms. Some researchers believe this creates greater international understanding by exposing individuals to different cultures and perspectives.

At the same time, others argue that globalization can threaten local languages, customs, and artistic traditions. Smaller cultures sometimes struggle to compete with the global influence of large entertainment industries and multinational corporations. Critics worry that cultural diversity may decline if local traditions are replaced by standardized global trends.

Globalization has also influenced migration and education. Students increasingly travel abroad for university studies, while international companies employ workers from multiple countries. These developments can encourage cooperation and innovation because people with different backgrounds contribute new ideas and experiences.

However, globalization has not benefited all groups equally. In some regions, factories moved production to countries with lower labor costs, causing unemployment in certain industries. Workers in developing countries may also face poor working conditions while producing goods for international markets. Economists therefore continue debating how governments should regulate trade and protect workers rights.

Technology has accelerated globalization further. The internet allows businesses to operate internationally and enables individuals to communicate instantly across continents. During global crises such as pandemics or climate-related disasters, countries often depend on international cooperation to share information and resources.

The flows are less one-directional than the debate often assumes. For much of the twentieth century, cultural export moved outward from a small number of wealthy countries, and the concern was straightforward: local film industries, music and languages losing ground to imports. That concern was reasonable, and in many places it was borne out.

The pattern since has become more complicated. South Korea, a country of around fifty million people, now exports music, television drama and film successfully to markets that previously exported to it. Nigeria's film industry produces more titles annually than Hollywood. Neither happened by accident: both were supported deliberately by governments that treated culture as an industry worth funding.

Researchers use the term glocalisation for a related pattern, in which an international product is altered substantially to fit a local market. The same fast food chain sells different menus on different continents; the same streaming service commissions drama in a dozen languages because subscribers prefer it.

Language remains the sharpest case, and here the concern is harder to dismiss. Roughly half of the world's seven thousand languages are expected to disappear within a century. A language does not usually die by being banned. It dies when parents make a rational decision that their children will do better speaking a larger one, which is a difficult thing to argue against, and impossible to reverse afterwards. By then the loss is counted in things nobody thought to write down.

Despite disagreements about its consequences, globalization remains one of the most influential forces shaping modern society. The challenge for future generations will likely involve balancing international cooperation with the protection of cultural diversity, social equality, and local identities.

title: The Development of Vaccines
text:
Vaccines are considered one of the most important achievements in medical history because they have prevented millions of deaths worldwide. By training the immune system to recognize harmful viruses or bacteria, vaccines reduce the spread of infectious diseases and protect both individuals and communities.

The history of vaccination began long before modern laboratories existed. In the eighteenth century, the English physician Edward Jenner observed that milkmaids who had been infected with cowpox rarely developed smallpox, a deadly disease that killed millions of people. Jenner used this discovery to develop one of the earliest vaccines, helping lay the foundation for modern immunology.

Since then, scientists have created vaccines against diseases such as polio, measles, and tetanus. Mass vaccination campaigns have dramatically reduced infection rates in many countries, and smallpox became the first human disease to be completely eradicated through vaccination.

Despite these successes, vaccine development remains a complex and challenging process. Researchers must carefully test vaccines to ensure they are both safe and effective. Clinical trials often involve thousands of participants and may take years to complete. During global emergencies, however, governments and pharmaceutical companies sometimes accelerate research while still following scientific safety standards.

Public trust plays an important role in vaccination programs. Misinformation and conspiracy theories spread online have caused some individuals to question vaccine safety despite strong scientific evidence supporting their effectiveness. Health experts warn that declining vaccination rates can allow preventable diseases to return.

Ethical questions have also emerged regarding global access to vaccines. Wealthier countries often secure medical supplies more quickly than poorer nations, creating inequalities during health crises. International organizations therefore argue that cooperation is necessary to ensure fair distribution of vaccines worldwide.

Recent advances in biotechnology, including mRNA technology, may influence future vaccine development significantly. Vaccination protects people who have not been vaccinated, which is the part most often misunderstood. If enough of a population is immune, a pathogen cannot find new hosts quickly enough to sustain an outbreak, and transmission collapses. The proportion required depends on how contagious the disease is: for influenza it is roughly forty per cent, for measles around ninety-five. Measles is unusually infectious, which is why it returns first whenever coverage drops.

That threshold matters most for people who cannot be vaccinated at all — newborns, patients undergoing chemotherapy, anyone with a compromised immune system. They depend entirely on the decisions of those around them.

Distribution is a separate problem from invention. Most vaccines require continuous refrigeration from factory to arm, and a single break in that cold chain destroys the dose without any visible sign. Several of the mRNA vaccines developed for COVID-19 initially required storage below minus seventy degrees, which made them impractical in much of the world until reformulation reduced the requirement.

Public confidence has its own history. A 1998 paper claiming a link between the MMR vaccine and autism was later shown to be fraudulent, and its author lost his medical licence. The study has been retracted for more than a decade. Vaccination rates in several countries have still not fully recovered, which suggests that a claim can outlive its own evidence by a considerable margin. Trust, once damaged, appears to rebuild far more slowly than it collapses.

Scientists hope these methods could allow faster responses to new diseases and even contribute to treatments for certain cancers.

Although debates about healthcare policies continue, most medical researchers agree that vaccines remain one of the most effective tools for protecting public health and preventing large-scale outbreaks.
